source.title: Minimum Increments to Equalize Leaf Paths

teaching.hint: When several child subtrees have different longest path totals, where can one increase affect all paths in a child subtree?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Each subtree can be equalized to its original longest leaf-path score; deficient children of a branching node each require one raise at their own root.
solution_outline.approach: Process the tree from leaves upward. For each node, find the maximum path sum through a child; count each child whose sum is smaller and carry the maximum plus this node’s cost upward.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The propagated value is the maximum original cost from that node to a leaf. Within a processed subtree, all paths can be equalized to this value using the counted raises.
solution_outline.correctness: Raising a deficient child by the gap lifts every leaf path beneath it at once, proving sufficiency. A path following maximum children within that deficient subtree must receive a positive raise; those witness paths for different deficient children are disjoint, giving a matching lower bound.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space; path sums may reach 10^14, so arithmetic must be wide.
solution_outline.pitfall: Counting the total increase instead of nodes changed solves a different optimization problem.

common_wrong_turns: Raise individual leaves instead of a shared ancestor
Minimize total increment rather than changed-node count
source_fidelity_notes: Clarified root-to-leaf score includes endpoints and objective counts distinct increased nodes; omitted image-dependent examples.
